issues: 'In 2015 Shoshana Zuboff named surveillance capitalism' reads as a claim that she coined the term in 2015. She did not. Zuboff first used it in her FAZ essay 'A Digital Declaration: Big Data as Surveillance Capitalism' (15 September 2014). Separately, Foster and McChesney had already published an article titled 'Surveillance Capitalism' in Monthly Review on 1 July 2014, using it in a different sense. I checked the Monthly Review page's <title> and its JSON-LD datePublished 2014-07-01; the body text is not in the served HTML. Wikipedia's 'Surveillance capitalism' article (--check FOUND) also says the term was 'popularized' by Zuboff and dates her essay to 2014. The 2015 JIT article develops the concept; it does not name it for the first time.

The quoted mechanisms that 'effectively exile persons from their own behavior' are, in the abstract, what constitutes 'Big Other'. That is the new expression of power produced by the architecture surveillance capitalism depends on, not surveillance capitalism itself. The statement assigns them to the logic of accumulation directly.

Minor: the institution field says 'Springer Nature'. The page metadata gives citation_publisher 'Palgrave Macmillan UK' (dc.publisher 'Palgrave') and dc.source 'Journal of Information Technology 2015 30:1'. The DOI now resolves to SAGE (journals.sagepub.com), which is the journal's current publisher. The Springer page date 2015-04-09 is right for that page, while Crossref gives the issue as March 2015. The page offers the abstract free, but the full text is subscription content.

fieldFixes.statement: In 2015 Shoshana Zuboff set out 'surveillance capitalism' (a term she had first used in a 2014 essay) as an emergent logic of accumulation, read through Google's practices, and argued that the architecture it depends on produces a new power she christened 'Big Other', made of mechanisms of extraction, commodification and control that 'effectively exile persons from their own behavior' while producing new markets of behavioural prediction and modification.

issues: The title is imprecise for 1991. In the original PGP 1.0 User's Guide (dated 'Version 1.0 - 5 Jun 91') this text is the section 'Why Do You Need PGP?'. 'Why I Wrote PGP' is the title of the later, revised essay, which the author's site describes as 'Part of the Original 1991 PGP User's Guide (updated in 1999)'.

The record's hedging note ('wording may differ from the 1991 original') can now be resolved. The 1991 guide, as preserved on the Internet Archive, contains 'If privacy is outlawed, only outlaws will have privacy.' verbatim. The email sentence differs slightly: 1991 reads 'private electronic mail (E-mail)', while the 1999 update reads '(email)'.

Context: in the 1999 online text the 'outlaws' line follows 'Throughout the 1990s, I figured...', which is later wording. In 1991 it followed the quotation of Senate Bill 266's 'sense of Congress' language.

issues: Causal conflation. The statement says privacy self-management fails 'because consent legitimises nearly any use of data and there are too many data collectors'. In Solove, 'Consent legitimizes nearly any form of collection, use, or disclosure of personal data' describes how the model works: it 'takes refuge in consent'. It is not one of his reasons for its failure. The reasons he gives are (1) 'severe cognitive problems' and (2) 'several structural problems', including that there are too many entities to manage one by one.

The quotes, the page (Volume 126, Issue 7, May 2013) and the 'since the 1970s' claim are correct. The page also has 'These rights consist primarily of rights to notice, access, and consent ...' and 'I will refer to this approach to privacy regulation as "privacy self-management."', which directly support 'named' and 'notice, access and consent'.

fieldFixes.statement: Solove (2013) named the dominant model 'privacy self-management' - rights to notice, access and consent, an approach largely unchanged since the 1970s, under which consent 'legitimizes nearly any form of collection, use, or disclosure of personal data' - and argued that it 'does not provide people with meaningful control' over their data, because of people's cognitive limits and structural problems: there are too many data collectors to manage one by one.
